p: The manuscript has pothēseis, "long for." Many editors change it to poiēseis, "make," as in Barnabas 19:12.

readings.w: Codex Constantinopolitanus (C, AD 1056), the one complete manuscript; Lake's text
readings.en: you shall not long for a split

readings.w: An emendation that, Lake says, "the editors usually" make; Barnabas 19:12 has the same line with ποιήσεις
readings.en: you shall not make a split

why: The manuscript's word makes good sense (do not even want division), and the Plain English Translation follows Lake's text, which keeps it. The change to "make" brings the line into line with Barnabas, but the two Two Ways texts differ in many small places, so agreement with Barnabas is not proof.

t: "This broken bread": a word Lake adds
p: The manuscript lacks the article "the" before "broken bread"; Lake adds it. The English is the same either way.

readings.w: Codex Constantinopolitanus (C): Lake's footnote, "τὸ om. C"

why: Greek normally puts the article between "this" and its noun, so Lake supplies it. The meaning does not change. The entry is here because the Plain English Translation follows Lake's text where Lake corrects the manuscript.

a: you are mighty. To you be the glory forever.
p: The manuscript reads "you" (sy) where Lake prints "to you" (soi). Harnack proposed keeping both.

readings.orig: ὅτι δυνατὸς εἶ· σοὶ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας
readings.en: because you are mighty; to you be the glory forever
readings.plain: you are mighty. To you be the glory forever.

readings.w: Codex Constantinopolitanus (C), as Lake's footnote reports it
readings.orig: ὅτι δυνατὸς εἶ· σὺ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας
readings.en: because you are mighty; you, the glory forever
readings.plain: you are mighty. You are the glory forever.

readings.w: Harnack's emendation, as Lake's footnote reports it
readings.orig: ὅτι δυνατὸς εἶ σύ· σοὶ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας
readings.en: because you are mighty, you; to you be the glory forever
readings.plain: you are mighty, you! To you be the glory forever.

why: Lake: C's σύ "is a common mistake for σοί" (the two sounded alike in later Greek), and "To you be the glory forever" is the refrain of these prayers (9:2, 9:3, 10:2). Harnack's proposal keeps C's word and adds the refrain.

p: The Greek manuscript praises "the God of David"; the Coptic fragment has "house of David," the Apostolic Constitutions "Son of David."

readings.w: Codex Constantinopolitanus (C, AD 1056), the one complete Greek manuscript; Lake's text. Kraft is unsure what the Georgian version reads here
readings.en: Hosanna to the God of David

readings.w: The Coptic fragment (fifth century, Didache 10:3-12:2), as Kraft reports it
readings.en: Hosanna to the house of David

readings.w: The Apostolic Constitutions, book 7, chapter 26 (fourth century), which rewrites the prayer; Kraft and the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation ("Hosanna to the Son of David")
readings.en: Hosanna to the Son of David

why: The Plain English Translation follows Lake's text, the only Greek witness to the whole prayer. "Son of David" is the crowd's cry in Matthew 21:9, so a later writer could easily bring the prayer into line with it; "God of David" is the harder reading.
b: Kraft suggests the original may have been "to David's Lord" (Psalm 110:1), which "easily could give rise to the three preserved readings," and compares Acts 7:46, where manuscripts differ between "house" and "God" of Jacob. Kraft also notes that in this verse the Coptic has "May the Lord come" (compare Revelation 22:20) and adds "Amen" in 10:4, 5 and 6.

p: The same letters can be split two ways: "Our Lord, come!" or "Our Lord has come." Lake prints the second.

readings.w: The same letters divided as μαράνα θά, as the SBLGNT divides them at 1 Corinthians 16:22
Lake's text, dividing μαρὰν ἀθά, as the Byzantine text does at 1 Corinthians 16:22
readings.en: Our Lord has come (or: is coming)

why: Ancient manuscripts were written without spaces, so the word division is the editor's choice, not the manuscript's. The prayer looks forward ("Let grace come, and let this world pass away"), and Revelation 22:20 gives the Greek of the same cry, "Come, Lord Jesus!" So the Plain English Translation divides the words as "Marana tha," as the site's 1 Corinthians 16:22 does, and departs from Lake here.

a: He is to stay only one day, and the next as well if there is need.
p: The manuscript lacks "except" (ei mē). Lake supplies it from 12:2.

readings.orig: οὐ μενεῖ δὲ εἰ μὴ ἡμέραν μίαν· ἐὰν δὲ ᾖ χρεία, καὶ τὴν ἄλλην
readings.en: he shall not stay except one day; if there is need, the next as well
readings.plain: He is to stay only one day, and the next as well if there is need.

readings.w: Codex Constantinopolitanus (C), as Lake's footnote reports it ("εἰ μή are omitted by C")
readings.orig: οὐ μενεῖ δὲ ἡμέραν μίαν· ἐὰν δὲ ᾖ χρεία, καὶ τὴν ἄλλην
readings.en: he shall not stay one day; if there is need, the next as well
readings.plain: He is not to stay one day, but the next as well if there is need.

why: Without "except" the sentence contradicts itself. Lake: "xii. 2 seems to make the correction quite certain," because 12:2 says the same of other travelers with εἰ μή ("not ... except two or three days").

p: The manuscript has a verb meaning "confess in addition"; Lake prints "confess beforehand."

readings.w: Codex Constantinopolitanus (C), as Lake's footnote reports it

why: The two Greek words differ by one letter. "Beforehand" fits the purpose clause that follows ("so that your sacrifice may be pure") and the rule of 4:14 (confess before prayer), so Lake corrects C.

p: The manuscript reads "our sacrifice"; Lake prints "your," as in 14:2.

readings.w: Codex Constantinopolitanus (C), as Lake's footnote reports it ("ἡμῶν C")

why: The whole chapter speaks to "you" ("your wrongs," "your sacrifice" in 14:2), and ἡμῶν and ὑμῶν were pronounced alike in later Greek, so copyists often confused them. Lake follows the context.
